summary.text: The identity matrix is a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else.
Multiplying by it is analogous to multiplying by the number 1, and as a geometric transformation it leaves every object unchanged.
It is its own inverse, and two square matrices multiply to give it exactly when each is the inverse of the other.

paragraphs.heading: Ones down the diagonal
paragraphs.text: For any size n, the identity matrix is the n × n square matrix with ones along its main diagonal and zeros in every other place. It is usually written Iₙ, or just I when the size does not matter or is clear from context. In the shorthand used for diagonal matrices, it is Iₙ = diag (1, 1, …, 1).

paragraphs.heading: The matrix version of 1
paragraphs.text: The identity matrix plays the part that the number 1 plays in ordinary multiplication. For any m × n matrix A, Iₘ A = A Iₙ = A. Used as a geometric transformation, it leaves every object just as it was. When n × n matrices stand for linear transformations of an n-dimensional space to itself, Iₙ stands for the identity function, whatever basis is used.

paragraphs.heading: Inverses
paragraphs.text: Among all n × n matrices, the identity matrix is the identity for multiplication. It is also the identity element of the general linear group GL(n), the group of all invertible n × n matrices under multiplication. Two square matrices multiply to give the identity matrix exactly when each is the inverse of the other. The identity matrix is invertible, and it is its own inverse.

paragraphs.heading: Columns and key numbers
paragraphs.text: Column i of the identity matrix is the unit vector eᵢ, which has a 1 in position i and 0 everywhere else. The determinant of the identity matrix is 1, its trace is n, and its rank is n. Using the Kronecker delta, it can be written (Iₙ)_ij = δ_ij.

paragraphs.heading: A surprise with square roots
paragraphs.text: Square roots of the identity matrix hold a surprise. Its principal square root is the identity matrix itself, and that is its only positive-definite square root. Yet once an identity matrix has two or more rows and columns, it has infinitely many symmetric square roots.

paragraphs.heading: Other names
paragraphs.text: Many writers have also called it the unit matrix, but identity matrix is now the standard term. Unit matrix is ambiguous, because it can also mean a matrix of ones or any unit of the ring of n × n matrices. In group theory or quantum mechanics the identity is sometimes a bold 1 or simply id. A few books write U, for unit matrix, or E, from the German word Einheitsmatrix.
